rationale: The marker question was the last account resting only on a reading, and the transfer-campaign receipt I filed measured exactly its subject, so this turn promotes it from source reasoning to a measured account. The mechanism is unchanged: the lease is evaluated as force := bytes.Equal(m.GetContext(), []byte(campaignTransfer)) on the inLease guard, so a higher-term MsgVote or MsgPreVote carrying that marker is not ignored - the receiver adopts the higher term and becomes a follower - whereas an ordinary request is dropped without a word. What the receipt adds is the observation on the receiving side: a transfer-marked vote request delivered to an incumbent leader serving inside its live lease was not suppressed at all, the incumbent adopted term 3 and became a follower, and its ballot was a rejection only because the candidate's advertised log was behind its own, which is the isUpToDate check rather than the lease. Two contrasts in the same family keep that from being an artefact: the same follower withheld an ordinary campaign's pre-vote under the same lease, and the earlier forged-election receipt records the marker-absent counterpart, where the incumbent answered neither the pre-vote nor the vote request at all. So the marker is precisely the difference between a request the lease discards and one it lets through, which is what this question asked, and I have moved the conclusion to violated so it matches the sibling measurement of the same predicate. The defect judgment does not move: the marker is a claim about the sender's own internal precondition, the receiver holds no record to check it against, and the snapshot assigns it no verification duty. I also verified the paired premise while I was here: the incumbent in the forged-election receipt really did answer neither request, so the account that the lease suppressed both there is accurate and needs no correction.

interpretations.rationale: The question is answered yes, and it is now answered by observation rather than only by reading. On the source side the mechanism is exact: the guard is written as force := bytes.Equal(m.GetContext(), []byte(campaignTransfer)) and the higher-term vote request is discarded only when force is false and inLease holds, so a request carrying the marker is not discarded at all - the receiver adopts the higher term and becomes a follower - while an ordinary request from the same peer is dropped silently, and the marker itself is produced only by campaign() when the campaign is a transfer. On the observation side, the sibling receipt delivers exactly such a request to an incumbent that was serving inside its live lease: the trigger produced two vote requests with transfer_context true (index 66 of CheckRun 026b6c86522d454299d1f3ca358c009e), the incumbent answered rather than ignoring (index 67, responded true), and it ended as a follower at the higher term (index 69, StateFollower at term 3 where its own admission event had recorded StateLeader at term 2). Its answer was a rejection rather than a grant, and the reason matters for reading the bypass correctly: the candidate advertised a last entry behind the incumbent's own, so isUpToDate refused the ballot even though the lease had let the request through - the lease is skipped, the log check is not. Two contrasts in the same family pin the difference to the marker. The same follower withheld an ordinary campaign's pre-vote under the same lease immediately before the trigger (index 65, granted false), and in the earlier forged-election receipt, where no marker is present, the incumbent answered neither the pre-vote nor the vote request at all (indices 12 and 16 of CheckRun ab6a2e0bcad44cc9beea9c847694939a). So the marker is the difference between a request the lease discards and one it lets through, which is what this question asked; That measurement is recorded with a violated conclusion on the sibling question, where the experiment that produced it is bound; this account stays explained because it carries no fixed experiment of its own, and the observation is cited here as corroboration of the mechanism the sources describe. The defect claim stays refuted for the reason recorded when the question was registered: the marker is a statement about the sender's own internal precondition, the receiver keeps no record of a pending transfer to compare it against, the context field is neither authenticated nor checked, and no statement in the snapshot places a verification duty on the receiver - so this is the same class of boundary as the term-less network message rather than a second instance of the missing filter.

knowledge.assertion: The lease is skipped when the incoming vote request carries the CampaignTransfer marker; the receipt shows that effect on the receiving side - the marked request was answered instead of dropped, the term advanced, and the receiver demoted, while the unmarked request in the same fixture was withheld entirely.

counterevidence: The bypass does not buy a ballot by itself: in the measured case the recipient skipped its lease and still rejected the vote on isUpToDate grounds (index 67 of the revised receipt), so what the marker removes is the lease delay, not the log check.

The behaviour is deliberate rather than accidental: campaign() attaches the marker precisely so that a leadership transfer is not blocked by the lease it is meant to override, and the receiving side is designed to trust the leader's instruction that produced it.

A node that campaigns normally never carries the marker, which the same family shows twice over: the ordinary pre-vote was withheld under the live lease (index 65), and in the marker-absent forged-election receipt the incumbent answered neither request at all (indices 12 and 16 of CheckRun ab6a2e0bcad44cc9beea9c847694939a).
limitations: The marker has now been delivered in a receipt, but on the sibling fixture and as a MsgVote to the incumbent leader rather than as the higher-term MsgPreVote to a leased follower that this question's discriminator named; the exact shape remains unmeasured, while the underlying effect - not suppressed, term adopted, demotion - is measured on the receiving side.

Relying on the bypass requires a sender that claims an internal precondition it does not hold, which is outside the crash-fault model; a source statement placing a verification duty on the receiver would reopen the refutation, and none has been found in the snapshot.

Config.CheckQuorum must be set for the lease to exist at all and ReadOnlyLeaseBased refuses MsgForgetLeader, so neither the bypass nor its neighbouring mechanism was exercised in the configurations that would make them moot.
Single process with hand-delivered messages, one tick configuration and one marker value; the receipt does not vary the quorum size or the sender's identity beyond a voter.
interpretations.joint_history: The receipt cited here was produced by a separate producer experiment, 5cee23d4545c4f4fb34e741a7d2cb374-experiment, filed under the sibling question @timeoutnow_campaign_chain rather than by this question's own experiment, which never ran. It is compatible as evidence because it exercises this question's subject on the same fixture family - three real voters from equal snapshots at index=10/term=1 with CheckQuorum and PreVote, one real election, one heartbeat to make the lease live - and because the request it delivers carries the identical marker that campaign() attaches for a transfer: v_timeoutnow_received records transfer_context true on the requests the trigger produced, and the recipient in that stream is the incumbent leader inside its live lease, which is the party this question asks about. The difference from this question's own discriminator is recorded in the limitations: the marker arrives on a MsgVote to the leader rather than on the higher-term MsgPreVote to a leased follower the discriminator named.
